The package manager is really the only main aspect of a particular distro. So basically we are going to a single distro system? Even between debian and ubuntu that use the same apt system the defining difference is the repository you have them hooked up to.

Maybe this is good maybe this is bad to drop the concept of a distro. It might make linux less confusing to newcomers if linux is just a single concept. It also might kill distro supported development because different distros help support different aspects of development (bleeding-edge vs stability vs usability). They feed back into that aspect of a software.

Your distro is more about what packages and default apps ship with the installer. Updaters can be swapped out, and you can force different distributions to use different repository methodologies, if that's really your thing. But there's no real, tangiblle difference between, say Ubuntu, LUbuntu, KUbuntu, and even Mint, beyond the default package/DE configurations -- and, as stated, getting YUM to run on any of them is trivial.

What I personally really like about Snap is the ability to have a universal rollback plan. Right now, if you're patching in a production environment, your rollback plans are a mix of various remove/uninstall statements, restoring from backup, restoring VM snapshots, breaking mirrors, etc. With a universal updater that provides true rollback capability, all that goes away; I can have one go-to option for backing out patches that fubar prod boxes, and that makes everyone happy.
